title: The Abomination in the Temple
sum: The book opens fast. In nine verses Alexander the Great conquers Persia, dies, and leaves his empire to generals whose heirs fill the earth with evils. From one of these lines comes "a sinful root," Antiochus IV Epiphanes, king from 175 BC. At the same time renegades in Jerusalem urge a covenant with the nations; with the king's leave they build a gymnasium, hide their circumcision and "sell themselves to do evil."

Antiochus invades Egypt, then turns on Jerusalem in 169 BC and strips the Temple of its gold altar, lampstand, table and ornaments. Two years later his officer sacks the city and fortifies the Citadel, a foreign garrison beside the sanctuary. Then the king decrees that all his kingdom be one people. In Judea that means an end to sacrifice, Sabbath, feasts and circumcision, with idols and pig sacrifice in their place, and death for anyone who refuses. In December 167 BC an "abomination of desolation" is built on the altar; scrolls of the law are burned; mothers who circumcised their sons are killed with their babies. Many die rather than eat unclean food, and "a very great wrath" falls on Israel.
readings: The chapter compresses eight years (175–167 BC) into a sequence of causes: Greek rule, Jewish renegades, a king's greed and pride, a decree. Historians test each link against 2 Maccabees, Daniel, Polybius and Josephus, and debate the biggest question it raises: why a Greek king, whose empire held many religions, tried to abolish one of them.

Twice the prose breaks into poetry (1:25–28; 1:36–40). The laments borrow the voice of Lamentations and the prophets, so that the reader mourns the Temple as Israel mourned it after Babylon. The chapter ends not with an answer but with wrath, and waits for chapter 2.

views.C: Catholic readers take the chapter as a true record of persecution for the faith, and the Church honors those who died rather than break the law: the Roman Martyrology keeps 1 August for the Holy Maccabean Martyrs of 2 Maccabees 7. Jerome's Commentary on Daniel, standard in the Latin West, reads Daniel 11 against these events and treats Antiochus as a type of the Antichrist to come.
views.P: Protestant readers who do not take 1 Maccabees as Scripture still value the chapter as the best account of the events Daniel 8 and 11 describe. Luther's 1533 preface said the book would not have been unworthy to be counted among the books of Scripture, because it is so useful for understanding Daniel 11, though it is not in the Hebrew Bible.
views.H: Historians accept the main events and much of their order, but not the book's explanation. Bickerman argued that Jerusalem's Hellenizing leaders, not the king, devised the new cult; Tcherikover that the decrees answered a Jewish revolt already under way; others stress Antiochus's need for money and loyal subjects. The "one people" decree for the whole kingdom (1:41) has no support outside Jewish sources.
views.J: The rabbis rarely tell this history, but they remember its themes: the Mishnah counts among the calamities remembered on the fast of 17 Tammuz that an idol was set up in the Temple (Mishnah Taanit 4:6), without saying when, and Megillat Ta'anit, an Aramaic list of feast days from the first century AD, marks Hasmonean victories as days when fasting is forbidden. The Scroll of Antiochus, whose date is debated (estimates run from the 2nd to the 7th century AD), retells the persecution for reading at Hanukkah.

deep.b:
On 15 Kislev 145 (December 167 BC) the king's men "built an abomination of desolation on the altar" (1:54), and ten days later they sacrificed on "the pagan altar that stood on top of the altar of sacrifice" (1:59). The phrase is Daniel's (Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11; compare Daniel 9:27), and the writer uses it as if his readers would know it. What exactly was built is not said. Most scholars think it was a Greek-style altar, perhaps with sacred stones, set on top of the old altar of burnt offering. 2 Maccabees 6:2 says the Temple was renamed for Olympian Zeus.

The Hebrew phrase in Daniel, shiqquts shomem, may be a pun. Eberhard Nestle suggested in 1884 that it mocks Baal Shamem, "Lord of Heaven," the Syrian name for the high god whom Greeks called Zeus: baal ("lord") becomes shiqquts ("detestable thing"), and shamem ("heaven") becomes shomem ("desolating"). Many scholars accept the pun.

Jesus' warning about "the abomination of desolation" standing in the holy place (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14) took the phrase into Christian teaching on the last days. Whether his words point to Antiochus's altar as a pattern, to the Roman destruction of AD 70, or to a future Antichrist, the churches differ; the card below sets out their answers. On the little horn of Daniel 7–8 and the Antichrist, see the card on the chapter 6 page and the card at Revelation 13.

The book's answer is simple: Antiochus was proud and greedy (1:21–24), and he wanted all "to be one people" (1:41). Historians find this hard to accept as it stands. Hellenistic kings usually left local religions alone, and no other people in the kingdom is known to have been forced to give up its gods. Antiochus's own father had guaranteed the Jews' right to live by their laws (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–144).

Three explanations have been offered. Elias Bickerman (The God of the Maccabees, 1937) argued that the persecution was the work of Jewish extremists of the Greek party, led by the high priest Menelaus, who wanted to reform Judaism into a Syrian cult without its "separatist" laws; the king backed them. Victor Tcherikover (Hellenistic Civilization and the Jews, 1959) argued that the order came after a revolt in Jerusalem (2 Maccabees 5:5–11), as punishment of rebels whose religion was the heart of their resistance. Martin Hengel (Judaism and Hellenism, 1974) gave weight to both. 1 Maccabees itself hints at the first view when it blames the renegades (1:11–15, 43, 52), and 2 Maccabees blames Jason and Menelaus at length (2 Maccabees 4:7–50).

The book dates events by "the kingdom of the Greeks" (1:10), the Seleucid era that began when Seleucus I took Babylon in 312/311 BC. Babylonian reckoning started the year in spring 311, Macedonian reckoning in autumn 312. Many scholars think 1 Maccabees uses the spring reckoning for Temple and Jewish events and the autumn one for royal events; others think it uses one system throughout. Either way the results are close: Antiochus became king in 175 BC (1:10), robbed the Temple in 169 (1:20), and the altar was defiled in December 167 (1:54). The Plain gives the book's own year numbers, and the notes give the dates BC.

echoes: Daniel 8:5–8; Daniel 8:23–25; Daniel 11:21–35; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 12:11; Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14; Lamentations 1:1–4; Lamentations 1:10; Amos 8:10; Jeremiah 36:23; Genesis 17:10–14; Leviticus 11:7; Psalm 74:3–8; Psalm 79:1; Isaiah 63:18

settings.to: many in Jerusalem, whom they "won over"
settings.when: early in Antiochus's reign, about 175 BC
settings.why: To persuade the people that separation from the nations had brought them harm, and that a covenant with the Greek world would bring them prosperity. The book gives the speech in one line, as the voice of the enemy within.
settings.readers: 2 Maccabees 4:7–15 names the leader as Jason, who bought the high priesthood and built the gymnasium. The book's first readers lived under Hasmonean rulers who had themselves taken Greek names, and Josephus says Aristobulus I (104–103 BC) was called "Philhellene," lover of the Greeks (Antiquities 13.318). Many scholars note that the writer's hard line against a "covenant with the nations" could be read as a warning to his own rulers.
views: Most historians accept that a strong Hellenizing party existed among Jerusalem's priests and leading families, as both books of Maccabees say.
Others note that the book gives the renegades no reasons beyond greed and gives no voice to Jews who hoped to keep the law and live as Greeks too.

settings.by: the writer, in the voice of Israel's mourners
settings.to: the reader, as a dirge over the people
settings.when: after Antiochus robbed the Temple in 169 BC
settings.why: To mourn the robbery as a national calamity, using the forms of Lamentations and the prophets: the groaning of elders, the fainting of the young, the silenced wedding.
settings.readers: Most scholars think the lament was composed in Hebrew with the rest of the book, probably by the writer himself; no Hebrew text survives, but Jerome says he found the first book of Maccabees in Hebrew (Prologus galeatus), and the pairs of parallel lines show through the Greek. Readers around 100 BC knew the Temple as rebuilt and splendid, so the poem asks them to remember how close it came to loss.

settings.when: after the Citadel was built and garrisoned in 167 BC
settings.why: To show what the Citadel meant: a constant ambush against the sanctuary, blood shed around it, the city deserted by its own children. The last lines echo Amos 8:10, "I will change your festivals into mourning."
settings.readers: For the book's first readers the Citadel was recent memory: it stood until Simon took it in 141 BC and made the day a feast (13:49–52). They knew the poem's "ambush" had lasted more than twenty-five years.

settings.to: "his whole kingdom," and by letters to Jerusalem and the towns of Judah
settings.when: 167 BC
settings.why: In the book's account, to make all the kingdom "one people": to end the law's worship and force on Judea the sacrifices and customs of the nations, on pain of death. The writer gives the decree as a list of the law's commands turned upside down.
settings.readers: No copy of the decree survives outside Jewish sources. 2 Maccabees 6:1–11 tells of the same measures, sent through "an elderly Athenian," and Daniel 7:25 speaks of a king who will "plan to change times and law." Readers who knew Daniel would have heard the decree as the fulfillment of that vision.
views: A decree for the whole empire
The book says the king wrote to "his whole kingdom" (1:41); some readers take this at face value.
Most historians think the decrees were aimed at Judea alone, and that the book's "whole kingdom" generalizes from Judea or reflects the king's call for unity in some other form.

traditions.q: Jesus warned of "the abomination of desolation" standing in the holy place (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14), the phrase 1 Maccabees uses for the altar of 167 BC (1:54). Was he pointing to the Roman destruction of AD 70, to a future Antichrist, or to both? (Whether Daniel's little horn is Antiochus or a final Antichrist is asked on the chapter 6 page; whether the Antichrist is the papacy, at Revelation 13.)
views: More than one reading. Jerome, on Matthew 24:15, said the words could be taken simply of the Antichrist, or of the image of Caesar that Pilate set in the Temple, or of Hadrian's equestrian statue placed on the site of the holy of holies.

Both. John Chrysostom, preaching on Matthew 24, took the abomination as the statue of the conqueror who took the city, set up in the Temple by the one who laid it waste in AD 70 (Homily 75). Cyril of Jerusalem taught those preparing for baptism that the Antichrist will come at the end and sit in the temple at Jerusalem (Catechetical Lecture 15.15), which agrees with the Orthodox row on the chapter 6 card.

AD 70. Calvin held that "abomination" means profanation: Christ warned that the Temple, once cleansed of the pollutions of Antiochus, would be profaned again by the Romans, and that its ruin would follow.

Still to come. Matthew 24:15 marks the middle of a future seven-year tribulation, when a ruler sets up an idol in a rebuilt temple, as 2 Thessalonians 2:4 describes. AD 70 did not fulfill it, because Jesus ties it to the great tribulation and his coming (Matthew 24:21, 29–30).
AD 70. Uriah Smith took the abomination in Jesus' words to be the pagan Roman armies standing around Jerusalem, as Luke's parallel shows (Luke 21:20). On the papacy, see the card at Revelation 13.

title: Mattathias's Zeal
sum: A priest named Mattathias has moved with his five sons from Jerusalem to Modein. He mourns the ruin of the city and the Temple in a lament. When the king's officers come to Modein and urge him, as the town's leading man, to sacrifice first and be rewarded as a Friend of the King, he refuses for himself and his family. A Jew steps forward to sacrifice. Mattathias kills him on the altar, kills the king's officer, tears down the altar, and calls everyone zealous for the law to follow him into the hills.

In the desert, a thousand faithful Jews let themselves be killed rather than fight on the Sabbath. Mattathias and his friends decide that they will defend themselves on the Sabbath. The Hasideans join them; they tear down altars, circumcise boys by force and strike down the lawless. Dying in 166 BC, Mattathias charges his sons with a speech that recalls the heroes of faith from Abraham to Daniel, names Simon as their counselor and Judas as their commander, and tells them to repay the nations.
readings: The chapter gives the Hasmonean family its charter. Mattathias is a priest, a new Phinehas whose zeal earned an everlasting priesthood (2:26, 54), and his dying words assign roles to Simon and Judas. Readers under Simon's heirs would have seen their rulers' legitimacy rooted here.
Read as a debate about the law

The chapter holds two kinds of faithfulness side by side: the thousand who die keeping the Sabbath (2:29–38) and Mattathias's decision to fight on it (2:39–41). The book honors both, but it is clear which one saved Israel.

views.C: Catholic readers have honored Mattathias as a model of fidelity under persecution. Ambrose of Milan praised the Maccabees' courage in defending the law, and Thomas Aquinas cited Mattathias's decision to fight on the Sabbath (2:41) as showing that a just war may be waged on holy days when necessity demands (Summa Theologiae II-II q.40 a.4).
views.P: Some Protestant readers admire Mattathias's refusal (2:19–22) as a pattern of conscience against the state, and are wary of his zeal: the killing at the altar and the forced circumcisions (2:24, 46) are not presented in the New Testament as a model for the church, which is told to suffer rather than use the sword for the faith (Matthew 26:52; 1 Peter 2:21–23).
views.H: Historians accept that the revolt began in the countryside under a priestly family from Modein, though 2 Maccabees does not mention Mattathias at all and starts with Judas (2 Maccabees 5:27). Many think the book enlarges the father's role to give the dynasty a priestly founder. The decision on Sabbath warfare is accepted as historical; Josephus repeats it (Antiquities 12.276–277).
views.J: The rabbis made the Hasmonean rule part of law: saving life overrides the Sabbath. The Babylonian Talmud reads Exodus 31:14, "because it is holy for you," as "the Sabbath is handed over to you, not you to the Sabbath" (Yoma 85b), and later law allows fighting on the Sabbath against an attack on a town. The prayer Al ha-Nissim, said at Hanukkah, begins "In the days of Mattathias son of Johanan, the high priest, the Hasmonean, and his sons."

deep.b:
The book models Mattathias on Phinehas, the priest who killed an Israelite and his Midianite partner at Peor and so turned God's anger away (Numbers 25:6–13). The words are almost the same: Mattathias "was zealous for the law, as Phinehas had been against Zimri son of Salu" (2:26), and his testament recalls that Phinehas "received the covenant of a holy priesthood" (2:54). Psalm 106:30–31 says that Phinehas's act "was reckoned to him as righteousness," and Sirach 45:23–24 praises him as third in glory after Moses and Aaron.

The comparison matters for the family's claim. Phinehas's reward was a priesthood for his descendants; the Hasmoneans were priests, though not of the line that had held the high priesthood. Their zeal was their title. Later Jews who took up arms against Rome also appealed to Phinehas and called themselves "zealots"; Martin Hengel traced the line from Phinehas through the Maccabees to them (The Zealots). On whether Phinehas's act was righteousness by works or by faith, see the card at Psalm 106; on Christians and the sword, the cards at Deuteronomy 20 and 1 Samuel 24.

The thousand in the desert refused to fight on the Sabbath and died "in our integrity" (2:37). The law forbade work on the seventh day (Exodus 20:8–11), and some Jews took this to include all fighting; Jubilees, from the same century, lists making war among things forbidden on the Sabbath on pain of death (Jubilees 50:12). Mattathias and his friends decided otherwise, but only for defense: "Whoever comes to make war on us on the Sabbath day, we will fight him" (2:41).

The limit held for a long time. Josephus says that Pompey took the Temple in 63 BC by building his siege works on Sabbaths, when the Jews would defend themselves only against a direct attack (Antiquities 14.63). The rabbis later grounded the principle in the law itself. Of God's rules Leviticus 18:5 says, "If a human being does them, he will live by them"; that means, they said, live by them and not die by them (Babylonian Talmud Yoma 85b). Jesus asked a similar question about healing: "Is it allowed on the Sabbath to do something good, or something bad? To save a life, or to kill?" (Mark 3:4). On whether Christians must keep the Sabbath, see the cards at Exodus 20 and Nehemiah 13.

Mattathias's list of heroes begins, "Abraham: was he not found faithful in the test, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness?" (2:52). The line joins two passages: the testing of Abraham at the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22:1) and the promise of Genesis 15:6, "Abram put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness." Sirach 44:20 makes the same link, "when he was tested he was found faithful."

The New Testament takes up both sides. James 2:21–23 asks, "Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered his son Isaac on the altar?" and then quotes Genesis 15:6. Paul quotes the same verse to argue that Abraham was counted righteous by faith before he was circumcised, and before any work (Romans 4:1–12). Mattathias's reading is close to James's, and many interpreters think James knew this tradition. How faith and works relate in justification is set out on the cards at Genesis 15 and Psalm 106.

echoes: Numbers 25:6–13; Psalm 106:30–31; Sirach 45:23–24; Deuteronomy 13:6–10; Exodus 22:20; Genesis 22:1; Genesis 15:6; James 2:21–23; Romans 4:3; Hebrews 11:17; Hebrews 11:33–34; Genesis 49:1–28; Deuteronomy 33:1; 1 Kings 2:1–9; Daniel 3:16–28; Daniel 6:22; 2 Kings 2:11; Lamentations 1:1; Mark 3:4

settings.to: no one in the story; it is spoken aloud, "Woe is me"
settings.when: after he moved to Modein, during the persecution of 167 BC
settings.why: To mourn the ruin of Jerusalem and the Temple, and to show why the priest will act: life is not worth living under such shame (2:13).
settings.readers: The lament sets up Mattathias as a figure like Jeremiah, who also asked why he was born (Jeremiah 20:18). Readers under his descendants heard the family's founder grieving before he fought, which gave the later wars the character of a holy cause rather than ambition.

settings.to: Mattathias, before the people of Modein
settings.when: at the sacrifice the officers had come to enforce (2:15)
settings.why: To win the town's leading man with honors: rank as a Friend of the King, silver, gold and gifts. If he sacrificed first, the town would follow.
settings.readers: The offer names the court rank, Friend of the King, that the Hasmoneans themselves later accepted from Seleucid kings (10:20, 65; 11:27). The book's first readers knew that the family later took these honors, but only after it had won the right to keep the law.

settings.to: the king's officers, in a loud voice, before the town
settings.when: in answer to the offer
settings.why: To refuse in public, for himself, his sons and his brothers: even if every nation obeys the king, they will keep the covenant of their ancestors and not turn aside from it.
settings.readers: The refusal echoes Joshua's "I and my family will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:15) and the three young men's refusal before Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3:16–18). Readers who knew Daniel, written in the same crisis, would have heard Mattathias as one of the faithful who "will be strong and take action" (Daniel 11:32).

settings.to: everyone in Modein "zealous for the law"
settings.when: right after he killed the apostate and the officer
settings.why: To gather the faithful around him; the words recall Moses' call after the golden calf, "Whoever is on the LORD's side, to me!" (Exodus 32:26), when the Levites killed the idolaters.
settings.readers: The first readers lived under the descendants of the men who answered this call. The call's echo of Exodus 32:26, where the Levites' zeal against the idolaters won them their priestly office (Exodus 32:29), supported the standing of a priestly family that was not of the old high-priestly line.
views: Josephus tells how the revolt against Rome in AD 66 began when priests refused the sacrifices for foreigners (War 2.409), and Hengel traced a line of zeal from Phinehas through Mattathias to the rebels.
Others read the call as the story of the founders, not a pattern for new wars.

settings.by: the faithful who had gone down to the desert
settings.to: the king's men who had come to attack them
settings.when: on a Sabbath day, early in the revolt
settings.why: To refuse the king's word and keep the Sabbath, even at the cost of their lives, and to call heaven and earth to witness that they died innocent.
settings.readers: 2 Maccabees 6:11 tells of a similar massacre of Jews keeping the Sabbath in caves. The first readers honored these dead, but the book uses their story to justify the decision that follows: such deaths would end Israel (2:40).

settings.what: The decision to fight on the Sabbath
settings.when: after they mourned the thousand dead
settings.why: To save the people from being wiped out: they will fight back if attacked on the Sabbath, though not start a battle.
settings.readers: The rule was still kept in the writer's day and long after (Josephus, Antiquities 14.63). Some groups, such as the community of the Dead Sea Scrolls, held stricter Sabbath rules; readers who knew of such disputes would have seen the book defending the Hasmonean practice.

settings.when: in 146 of the Seleucid era (166 BC), shortly before his death
settings.why: To pass on the cause: to urge zeal for the law, to give examples of God's faithfulness to those who kept faith, from Abraham to Daniel, and to appoint Simon as counselor and Judas as commander.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Judeans in the generation after Simon (about 130–90 BC), ruled by Simon's son John Hyrcanus or his grandsons. They heard their dynasty's founder naming Simon as "a father to you" (2:65), which supported the line that actually ruled. The list of heroes, like Sirach 44–50 and Hebrews 11, shows how the sacred history was being read as a gallery of examples.
views: Many scholars think the testament was written to show that Simon, ancestor of the ruling house, was chosen from the start.
Others think the speech gathers what the family remembered of Mattathias's words, recast in the writer's style, as ancient historians usually did.

title: Judas Takes Command
sum: Judas Maccabeus takes his father's place, and a hymn of praise likens him to a lion and a giant. He kills Apollonius, governor of Samaria, and takes his sword; he routs Seron's larger army at the pass of Beth-horon, telling his hungry men that victory does not depend on numbers, because strength comes from Heaven.

Angry at the news and short of money, Antiochus goes east to raise tribute, leaving Lysias as regent with half the army and orders to wipe out Judea and resettle it with foreigners. Lysias sends Ptolemy, Nicanor and Gorgias with a great army to Emmaus, and slave dealers come to buy captives. Judas gathers the people at Mizpah, as Samuel once did, to fast, pray and spread out the scroll of the law; with the Temple defiled, they lay its offerings before Heaven and ask what to do. He organizes the army as Moses did, sends home those the law exempts, and tells the rest to be ready: whatever Heaven wills, he will do.
readings: The chapter follows the pattern of Israel's wars in Joshua, Judges and Samuel: a small band, a prayer, the law's exemptions, a speech, a victory. Judas says the theology out loud (3:18–22), and the book shows it working.

The same chapter is full of practical detail: the guerrilla ambush at the pass, the enemy's divided command, the slave dealers in the camp. Historians such as Bar-Kochva find in it a credible picture of how a small army beat Seleucid forces in the hills.

views.C: Catholic writers have read Judas as a model of the Christian soldier who fights with prayer. In the Middle Ages he was counted among the Nine Worthies, with Joshua and David, as one of the three heroes of the Old Testament. Thomas Aquinas cited Mattathias's decision to fight on the Sabbath (2:41) when he asked whether war may be waged on holy days (Summa Theologiae II-II q.40 a.4).
views.P: Protestant readers have often drawn on this chapter for the lesson that God gives victory to the faithful few, setting Judas's "strength comes from Heaven" (3:19) beside 1 Samuel 14:6 and 17:47. They also note that the book, unlike 2 Maccabees, tells of no visions or miracles in battle.
views.H: Historians judge the military narrative largely reliable in outline. The enemy numbers are inflated, and 2 Maccabees 8 tells the Emmaus campaign differently, with Nicanor as chief commander. The eastern campaign of Antiochus (3:31–37) is confirmed by Greek and Babylonian sources.
views.J: The Mizpah scene, with fasting, the law scroll and trumpets, matches the pattern of fasts for public danger in Mishnah Taanit, where the ark with the scroll is brought into the town square and ashes are put on it (Mishnah Taanit 2:1). Rabbinic tradition did not keep the story of Judas, but this pattern of public prayer before danger survived in Jewish practice.

deep.b:
The poem in 3:3–9 is a portrait in Hebrew style: a giant in armor, a lion's cub, a man who burns out the lawless and turns away wrath. It gathers images from Israel's oldest heroes. Judah is "a lion's cub" in Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:9); Phinehas turned away God's rage (Numbers 25:11); David killed the giant and took his sword (1 Samuel 17:51; compare 1 Maccabees 3:12). The last line, "he gathered those who were perishing" (3:9), gives Judas a shepherd's task.

Some scholars think the poem was written after Judas's death, since "his memory will be a blessing forever" (3:7) reads like an epitaph. Either way, it shapes how the reader sees the battles that follow: they are the deeds of a hero raised by God, not the luck of a guerrilla captain. The same hope for a lion of Judah took a different form in Revelation 5:5, where the Lion turns out to be a slain Lamb.

At Mizpah the people face a problem the law had not imagined: the Temple is defiled, but the law still requires firstfruits, tithes, priestly garments and the offerings of Nazirites whose vows are finished (3:49). They bring all of it to the old place of prayer and ask Heaven, "What are we to do with these? Where can we take them?" (3:50).

Three things fill the Temple's place: fasting and sackcloth (3:47), the scroll of the law spread open (3:48), and trumpets (3:54), which the law said would make God remember Israel in battle (Numbers 10:9). Many scholars see here an early form of the worship that later sustained Judaism without a Temple, gathered around the scroll and prayer. The meaning of 3:48 itself is uncertain; see the note.

Judas's speech at Beth-horon (3:18–22) states the book's theology of war: it is easy for many to be defeated by a few, Heaven saves by many or by few, and strength comes from Heaven. The words recall Jonathan at Michmash, "He can save with many or with few" (1 Samuel 14:6), and David before Goliath, "the LORD saves, and not by sword and spear" (1 Samuel 17:47).

The book holds this faith together with careful attention to tactics: the ambush in the pass, the night march at Emmaus, the fortified towns. It never tells of a miracle on the battlefield, unlike 2 Maccabees, where heavenly horsemen appear (2 Maccabees 10:29–30; 11:8). Heaven's help, in 1 Maccabees, comes through courage and good generalship. On Christians and war, see the card at Deuteronomy 20.

echoes: Genesis 49:9; Numbers 23:24; Numbers 25:11; 1 Samuel 17:47; 1 Samuel 17:51; 1 Samuel 21:9; 1 Samuel 14:6; 2 Chronicles 14:11; Joshua 10:10–11; 1 Samuel 7:5–11; Numbers 10:9; Exodus 18:21; Deuteronomy 20:5–8; Judges 7:3; 2 Samuel 10:12; Numbers 6:13–20; Lamentations 1:4; Isaiah 63:18; Daniel 11:44; Revelation 5:5; Matthew 6:10

settings.by: the writer, perhaps using an older poem
settings.when: at the start of Judas's command, 166 BC; possibly composed after his death in 160 BC
settings.why: To present Judas as a hero in the line of Judah, Phinehas and David, before telling his battles.
settings.readers: The book's first readers lived under Judas's nephews and great-nephews, and many scholars think the hymn kept alive a popular memory of him. 2 Maccabees, written for Jews in Egypt, praises Judas even more highly and almost ignores his brothers, which suggests that his fame spread beyond the family's own circle.

settings.by: Seron, commander of the army of Syria
settings.when: before marching on Judea, 166 BC
settings.why: To win fame by crushing Judas and those who scorned the king's word.
settings.readers: The boast sets up a reversal that the first readers knew from Israel's stories: the proud enemy who seeks a name falls before the humble (compare Genesis 11:4; 1 Samuel 17:44). Readers would hear "make a name" against Judas, whose "name was known to the end of the earth" (3:9).

settings.when: as Seron's army came up the pass
settings.why: To steady his men: numbers do not decide battles, Heaven does, and they are fighting for their lives and their laws.
settings.readers: The words would have been familiar to the first readers from 1 Samuel 14 and 17, and they knew the pass of Beth-horon as the place of Joshua's victory. Ambrose of Milan later praised the Maccabees' courage as an example of fortitude (On the Duties of the Clergy 1.40–41).

settings.to: Lysias, regent of the western provinces
settings.when: 165 BC, before the king left for the east
settings.why: To crush Israel, wipe out the remnant of Jerusalem, settle foreigners in the land and divide it among them.
settings.readers: The orders read as a reversal of the conquest under Joshua and a repetition of what Assyria did to Samaria (2 Kings 17:24). Daniel 11:39, written in the same years, speaks of a king who will "hand out the land for a price." Readers in the Hasmonean state, which had by then conquered Idumea and Samaria, knew how near Judea had come to that fate.

settings.what: The resolve to restore the people
settings.when: when they learned of the royal orders and the army at Emmaus
settings.why: To commit themselves to raise up the people and the sanctuary from ruin, the goal that chapter 4 reaches.
settings.readers: The feast this resolve led to was still being kept and urged on other Jews when the book was written (4:59; 2 Maccabees 1:9, 18), so its first readers heard here the first statement of the purpose their feast celebrated.

settings.when: as the people gathered at Mizpah, with Jerusalem in enemy hands
settings.why: To describe the emptied city and the silenced worship, and to explain why the people went to Mizpah.
settings.readers: The poem draws on Lamentations and Jeremiah, which the first readers heard as the words of the Babylonian ruin. Placing them here made the Maccabean crisis a second destruction, and the coming rededication a second return.

settings.when: after the fast and the reading of the law at Mizpah, 165 BC
settings.why: To lay before God the offerings that had nowhere to go, to describe the profaned sanctuary and the gathered nations, and to ask for help.
settings.readers: The prayer has the form of a community lament like Psalm 74 and Psalm 79, which many scholars date to the Babylonian ruin, though some have dated them to this crisis. The first readers, who prayed such psalms, would have heard their own prayers in it.
views: Some interpreters, ancient and modern, have read Psalms 44, 74 and 79 as written during the Maccabean persecution.
Most scholars think those psalms are older, and that the book's prayer borrows their language.

settings.to: the army, camped south of Emmaus
settings.when: the evening before the battle
settings.why: To ready his men for a fight at dawn, to tell them death is better than watching the nation's ruin, and to leave the outcome to the will of Heaven.
settings.readers: The last words echo Joab before the Ammonite war (2 Samuel 10:12). Christian readers of the KJV and Douay, which add "of God," heard in them the Lord's Prayer, "May your will be done, as in heaven" (Matthew 6:10).

title: The Temple Made Clean
sum: At Emmaus Gorgias marches by night to surprise Judas's camp, but Judas has already left it. At dawn he strikes the main enemy camp with three thousand poorly armed men, recalling the Red Sea and praying that Heaven will remember the covenant. The enemy flees; Judas holds his men back from plunder until Gorgias's force sees the burning camp and runs. They return singing, "For his loyal love is good forever." The next year Lysias comes with a larger army by the southern road and is beaten at Beth-zur after Judas prays, remembering David and Jonathan.

Judas and his brothers go up to Mount Zion and find the sanctuary deserted, its gates burned and weeds in the courts. They mourn, then set to work: soldiers hold off the Citadel, blameless priests cleanse the sanctuary, the defiled altar is torn down and its stones stored "until a prophet should come," and a new altar is built of uncut stones. On 25 Kislev 148 (December 164 BC), three years to the day after the profanation, they offer sacrifice and dedicate the altar with songs, harps and cymbals for eight days. The assembly decrees that the days be kept every year. The chapter ends with walls around Mount Zion and a fortress at Beth-zur.
readings: Everything in chapters 1–3 builds to this. The profaned altar of 1:54, the silenced harps of 3:45 and the question "Where can we take them?" (3:50) are answered: the altar is rebuilt, the music returns, the offerings have a place again.
Read as the origin of a feast

The chapter ends with a decree (4:59) that founded Hanukkah, a feast not commanded in the law of Moses. The writer's readers kept it every year, and he may have meant his story to be read as its explanation.

views.C: Catholic readers see in the cleansing and rededication the pattern of renewal of the Church's worship. The Church dedicates and consecrates its churches and altars with rites that recall Solomon's dedication and this one, and the weekday lectionary reads the rededication (4:36–59) in the last weeks of the Church's year.
views.O: Orthodox readers note that Jesus was in the Temple at "the Feast of Dedication" (John 10:22), and Orthodox churches keep feasts of the dedication of churches; on 13 September they keep the dedication of the Church of the Resurrection in Jerusalem, which the pilgrim Egeria, about AD 384, said was celebrated on the day Solomon's Temple had been dedicated.
views.P: Protestant readers value the chapter as the history behind John 10:22 and as an example of reforming worship by the law: the priests who "loved the law" (4:42), the uncut stones (4:47), the refusal to decide what the law does not reveal (4:46). Whether the church may keep feasts the law does not command, as Judas did, divides them; see the card below.
views.H: Historians accept the rededication in December 164 BC, about three years after the profanation, but note that 2 Maccabees counts two years (2 Maccabees 10:3) and puts the death of Antiochus IV before it (2 Maccabees 9–10). A Babylonian king list records that the news of the king's death was heard in Babylon in year 148, probably in Kislev (the month is restored). The order of Lysias's campaign and the rededication, and whether Lysias was beaten or negotiated, are debated.
views.J: Jews keep Hanukkah for eight days from 25 Kislev, lighting lamps each night. The Babylonian Talmud explains the eight days by a jar of pure oil that burned for eight days (Shabbat 21b), a story not in 1 Maccabees, and it says the feast was fixed "the next year" with praise and thanksgiving. 2 Maccabees 10:6 instead links the eight days to the Feast of Booths, and Josephus calls the feast "Lights" (Antiquities 12.325).

deep.b:
The cleansing follows the pattern of earlier reforms. Hezekiah's priests carried the uncleanness out of the Temple and finished on the eighth day (2 Chronicles 29:15–17); Solomon dedicated the altar for seven days and kept an eighth (2 Chronicles 7:8–9). Judas's men tear down the defiled altar, build a new one of whole stones as the law commands (Exodus 20:25), make new vessels, relight the lampstand and set out the bread. The date is the anniversary of the first pagan sacrifice (1:59; 4:54), so the restoration answers the profanation day for day.

The feast took its names from this chapter: Hebrew Hanukkah and Greek enkainia both mean "dedication" or "renewal" (4:36, 56, 59). 2 Maccabees opens with two letters urging the Jews of Egypt to keep it (2 Maccabees 1:1–2:18), and John records that Jesus walked in the Temple during it (John 10:22–23). The lamps, so central to the feast today, appear in 1 Maccabees only as the lampstand relit (4:50); Josephus says the feast was called "Lights" because the right to worship had shone out unexpectedly (Antiquities 12.325), and the story of the oil comes from the Talmud (Shabbat 21b). The feast's name echoes older dedications: "the dedication of the altar" in Numbers 7:10–11 and 7:84–88, Solomon's dedication of the house (1 Kings 8:63), and the title of Psalm 30, "A song for the dedication of the house."

The stones of the defiled altar raise a question no one can answer. They were holy, so they could not be thrown away; they had been defiled, so they could not be used. The priests store them "until a prophet should come to give a ruling about them" (4:46). The Mishnah remembers that the Hasmoneans hid the altar stones in a chamber of the Temple (Mishnah Middot 1:6).

The phrase shows a sense, shared by the writer, that no prophet was then speaking in Israel (also 9:27; 14:41). Later Jewish tradition said that prophecy ceased after Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi (Tosefta Sotah 13:3), and Josephus that the exact succession of prophets ended with Artaxerxes (Against Apion 1.41). Protestant and Catholic writers draw opposite conclusions from this for the canon; the question is set out in the card on the book page.

Bar-Kochva's study of the battles finds the account of Emmaus credible: a night march by Gorgias to catch the rebels in their camp, Judas's counter-march to the enemy's base, a dawn attack on a divided force. 2 Maccabees 8:23–36 tells the same battle with Nicanor as the commander and ends it on the eve of a Sabbath.

The battle of Beth-zur is harder. 1 Maccabees places Lysias's campaign before the rededication and ends it with Lysias retreating to raise more troops (4:35). 2 Maccabees 11:1–38 places it after the rededication and the death of Antiochus IV, and records letters of a negotiated settlement, including a letter of the young king restoring the Temple to the Jews. Many historians think some of these letters date from 164 BC, and that the rededication followed a truce. The two accounts conflict, and the book's version, in which Judas simply wins, may be shaped by its purpose.

echoes: Exodus 14:9–31; Exodus 2:24; 1 Samuel 17:46; 1 Samuel 14:1–23; Psalm 136:1; Psalm 118:1; 2 Chronicles 20:21; Joshua 2:11; Lamentations 5:18; Leviticus 14:40–45; Deuteronomy 18:18; Psalm 74:9; Exodus 20:25; Deuteronomy 27:6; Leviticus 24:2–9; 2 Chronicles 7:8–9; 2 Chronicles 29:15–17; Nehemiah 12:27; Ezra 6:16–17; Numbers 7:10–11; Numbers 7:84–88; 1 Kings 8:63–66; Psalm 30:1; Daniel 8:14; John 10:22–23

settings.when: at dawn, finding Judas's camp empty
settings.why: To explain the empty camp as flight; he is wrong, and the reader knows it.
settings.readers: 2 Maccabees, written for Jews in Egypt, tells this battle without Gorgias's night march (2 Maccabees 8:23–29), so the irony belongs to this book's own account for its Judean readers: the boast of a commander outwitted by a smaller force, like Goliath in the older story.

settings.when: at dawn, before attacking the enemy camp
settings.why: To turn fear into trust by remembering the Red Sea, and to ask that Heaven remember the covenant and show the nations that Israel has a redeemer.
settings.readers: The Exodus was retold every Passover, so the first readers knew the pattern well. The speech asks them to see their own history as a new exodus, a reading also found in Isaiah 51:9–11 and Psalm 106.

settings.when: after the first rout, with Gorgias still in the hills
settings.why: To keep his army together until the second enemy force is beaten.
settings.readers: The order shows a commander's sense, and readers who knew Achan's story (Joshua 7) or Saul's (1 Samuel 15) also heard obedience. 2 Maccabees 8:28 adds that the plunder was shared with widows and orphans, a detail aimed at readers who valued almsgiving.

settings.when: on the way back from the plunder of the camp
settings.why: To give thanks for the victory in the words of the Temple refrain.
settings.readers: The refrain "his loyal love is forever" was sung by Levites in the Temple (2 Chronicles 5:13; Ezra 3:11). Readers who heard it in Temple worship would notice that the army sings it while the Temple is still in enemy hands, as a promise of what follows.

settings.when: before the battle with Lysias, 164 BC
settings.why: To ask God to do again what he did by David and by Jonathan: give a strong army into the hands of a few.
settings.readers: The title "Savior" (Greek sōtēr) was also used by kings: Demetrius I, who would make war on Judas, took the name Soter. Readers who knew the royal titles would hear the prayer give to God the title that kings claimed.

settings.what: The decision to cleanse the sanctuary
settings.when: after Lysias withdrew
settings.why: To go up to Mount Zion, cleanse the sanctuary and dedicate it again, the goal named at 3:43.
settings.readers: For the first readers this verse began the story told each year at Hanukkah. Daniel 8:14, written in these years, promises that the sanctuary "will be made right" after a set time; readers who knew Daniel would have heard its fulfillment here.

settings.by: Judas, his brothers and the whole assembly of Israel
settings.to: all Israel, for every year to come
settings.when: at the rededication, Kislev 148 (December 164 BC)
settings.why: To keep the eight days of the altar's dedication every year with joy and gladness.
settings.readers: The first readers kept the feast; 2 Maccabees 1:9 and 1:18 show Judean leaders urging it on the Jews of Egypt, so the feast was a bond between the homeland and the diaspora. Some scholars think the book itself was meant partly to explain the feast and the family who founded it.
views: Many readers compare the decree with the founding of Purim by Mordecai and Esther (Esther 9:20–32), another feast set by Israel's leaders rather than by the law of Moses.
Some historians stress that the feast also honored the Hasmonean family, and note that the rabbis, who were cool toward the dynasty, retold it with a miracle instead of the family's deeds.

traditions.q: Judas and the assembly set up a yearly feast the law of Moses does not command (4:59), and Jesus was in the Temple at that feast (John 10:22). May the church set up holy days that neither Testament commands? (Whether God's people must keep a set calendar is asked on the 1 Enoch 82 card.)
views: Yes. The Code of Canon Law reserves to the supreme authority of the Church the power "to establish, transfer, and suppress feast days and days of penance common to the universal Church" (canon 1244), and the Catechism counts attending Mass on holy days of obligation among the precepts of the Church (paragraph 2042).

Yes. Beside Pascha the church keeps twelve great feasts, some of which mark events after the New Testament, such as the Exaltation of the Cross on 14 September; the church's feasts are part of the holy tradition it has received (Ware, The Orthodox Church).

Yes, as matters of good order. The Augsburg Confession says that rites which can be kept without sin and serve peace and good order, "such as particular holy-days, festivals, and the like," should be kept, but consciences must not be burdened as if they were necessary for salvation (article 15).

Yes. The church "hath power to decree rites or ceremonies" so long as nothing is ordained contrary to Scripture (article 20), and every particular church may ordain, change and abolish ceremonies "ordained only by man's authority" (article 34).

Divided. The Westminster Confession allows only the worship God has himself instituted (21.1), and the Westminster Directory's appendix keeps no holy day but the Lord's Day. The Second Helvetic Confession (chapter 24) instead approves highly of churches that, in Christian freedom, keep the memory of the Lord's nativity, circumcision, passion, resurrection and ascension and of the sending of the Spirit, but rejects feasts made for men or saints.
